This is the working document the worlds are built by, as it stands today. It says "game" where the site says "world", and names a few files; the rules and the research are what matter here.

Design principles

How re-kid's games should feel and what they must never do. They apply to every world and game; a game brief may add its own. The research behind them is at the end. Status and next steps are in docs/PROJECT_PLAN.md.

Calm and soothing, first

The first thing people outside the family said of the games (2026-10-31, via Adam) was that they calm and soothe. That is the effect to keep, and it comes before any other aim here: a new gag, creature, sound or feature that makes the scene busier, louder or more urgent loses it, however funny.

  • Gentle tempo. Slow movements, pauses between happenings, room to look. Life goes on in the background at its own pace; nothing demands attention.
  • Soft surprises. Mishaps and jokes land as a giggle, not a jolt: no sudden loud sounds, flashes or shaking screen. A fright in the story (a frog plopping in) is small, and settles at once.
  • One thing at a time. Never several happenings competing for the eye; ambient life is quieter and slower than what the child chose.
  • Warm characters. Kind to each other, never in real danger, never upset for long; every trouble ends in comfort or a shared laugh.
  • Quiet sound. Music low and slow, effects soft, long silences fine.
  • A slow wind-down. Evening is the calmest part of the day, as the scene gets ready for sleep.

Faithful to the original

  • True to the cartoon's character: its look, pacing, humour, music and emotional tone. The aim is to bring back the affection people have for these worlds, and to help them understand the worlds better.
  • Inspired by the original, not copied from it. Original sounds and melodies appear only as occasional easter eggs.
  • Restraint. Modern touches (responsive music, a changing sky, small details, expressive characters, things that react) add depth only if the game stays quiet, unhurried and recognisable. Study the original closely enough to know when to hold back.
  • Beautiful to look at, never loud or busy. Avoid effects that only distract.
  • Almost like watching the cartoon, and what only play can do (Adam, 2026-11-10). Check a gag, a left-alone move or a feature two ways. Would it pass as a moment from the film: staged, acted, a setup and a payoff, held long enough to read? And could the film not have done it: it happens because of the child, or differently because of them? Failing the first gives a toy (a fidget, a one-beat answer); failing the second, a cartoon to watch (a chain that plays on by itself). What play has that a film lacks: the child picks what is tried, the same again on demand, their own pace, the hero noticing them, the world answering a touch, and what was done staying for the day.

A little world, not a game to finish

  • A world to live in for a while. The child can wander, look, repeat a favourite thing many times, or do nothing. There is no right pace, and nothing has to be completed.
  • Time is the same for everyone. How long the day lasts never depends on how much is done. A child who spends the whole day watching a snail gets as long as one who tries everything. Curiosity leads to discoveries, never to an earlier bedtime.
  • Play needn't teach. Humour, surprise, repetition and make-believe are reason enough. A bowl stuck on Reksio's head is worth having because it is funny.
  • Mistakes are safe, and sometimes funny. No failure, no scores, no judging how well the child does.
  • A tap is the child's choice, not a skip. Where a character could try more than one thing, the child picks which by tapping it, and each try has its own understandable, often funny, result; one of them resolves it. Left alone, the character tries by himself, so watching is fine too. A tap that only hurries a scene on gives the child nothing to decide (the meadow's first encounters, 2026-10-16).
  • The character shows he heard. Every tap gets an answer at once, before any long move: a look towards what was tapped, a lean, then off. Acting, more than motion, makes it read as a cartoon; it never makes the child wait to be answered.
  • What can be tapped shows itself, to a mouse. On a computer, the thing under the pointer glows round its outline and the character turns to it, and the hand cursor shows only over what answers a click. Nothing is marked for a finger: on a phone or tablet the scene stays as drawn (children at a desktop couldn't tell what to click, 2026-10-20).
  • Nothing comes from nowhere, nothing vanishes. Every thing in a scene is brought by someone, comes on its own feet, or was always there, and leaves the same way: paint tins carried in and out by the hare and the mouse, the poles brought by birds, the toy car rolling in and breaking on the way. A visitor sent home walks off the screen, or ducks into its hole. A tap that cuts a gag short sends everyone home the same way. Things that fell from the sky and visitors that blinked out made the meadow's encounters feel random (Adam, 2026-10-23). The meadow checks it as it plays (friends.js: a visitor comes in from out of sight and goes home out of sight).
  • Kindness happens in the story. Characters help each other: Reksio helps, and sometimes he needs help. These are small stories, not lessons about being good.
  • Things from the child's own life. Use objects a child knows from home, such as Eliot's grandfather's wall clocks, even if he doesn't know what they are for yet.

Easy to finish

  • The same day every time: morning, day, evening, sleep. Because the routine is predictable, the end is expected, not imposed.
  • The ending is part of the story. Reksio is tired and goes to sleep; there is no limit set from outside the game. Eliot already accepts this.
  • No countdowns or hurry. A clock in the world tells the time; it never says time is running out, and nothing is lost when the day ends. No urgent music, flashing or warnings near the end.
  • A new play starts only when a parent chooses. No "play again" prompt, and a toddler's tap can't restart it. Restarting is something only a grown up would do.
  • Never designed to keep a child playing. No streaks, rewards for playing longer, things to collect, characters who ask the child to stay or come back, ads, or purchases. A short game a parent and child remember together is a success; a long session isn't.
  • What success looks like: laughter, the child trying things on their own, curiosity, things to talk about, play that carries on away from the screen, and an ending accepted calmly.

Made to be played together

  • A parent beside the child is the expected way to play. The games have no words, so the talking is the parent's: moments worth pointing at, asking about, laughing at together.
  • For parents, a way back to their own childhood: the cartoon, and the episode a gag comes from.

Is a few minutes a day fine for a toddler?

The question: is a game like this (a few minutes a day, a child of about 3, usually with a parent) fine to give him? Researched 2026-10-13. Short answer: yes, if it stays short, calm, free of manipulation, and played together, and not just before bed. What the sources say, then what follows for us.

What the guidance says

  • WHO (2019), children under 5: for ages 2 and 3–4, "sedentary screen time should be no more than 1 hour; less is better", and when sitting, "reading and storytelling with a caregiver is encouraged". For 1-year-olds it is not recommended. (WHO news release, 24 April 2019; the full guideline is ISBN 9789241550536.)
  • American Academy of Pediatrics, "Media and Young Minds" (Pediatrics 138(5), e20162591, 2016), ages 2–5: "limit screen use to 1 hour per day of high-quality programming, coview with your children, help children understand what they are seeing, and help them apply what they learn to the world around them." Also: "Letting children use media by themselves should be avoided"; "Avoid fast-paced programs …, apps with lots of distracting content, and any violent content"; "No screens 1 hour before bedtime"; and "Avoid using media as the only way to calm your child." It asks makers of apps for interfaces "that are not distracting, and that promote shared parent–child media use", and to remove advertising. (Read in full.)
  • UK Chief Medical Officers (2019): the evidence does not show screen use causing mental health problems, but that is not evidence of no effect; they advise caution and set no time limit, because screen time varies in quality, content and effect. (CMO commentary; read through summaries.)

A 5-minute day is about a twelfth of the WHO and AAP hour.

What the research says

  • Quality and playing together count, not just minutes. A meta-analysis of 42 studies (about 18,900 children) found more screen time linked to weaker language, and educational programmes and watching with a carer linked to better language. The links are small and correlational, the evidence was rated low quality, and most of the studies are about TV, not tablets. (Madigan et al., JAMA Pediatrics 174(7):665–675, 2020; abstract and summaries.)
  • Most apps for 3–5-year-olds are built to keep them playing. Of 133 apps used by 160 children aged 3–5, 80% had at least one manipulative design: characters pressing the child to keep playing, countdown time pressure, lures, menus that steer, ads. Only 26 apps had none. (Radesky et al., JAMA Network Open 5(6):e2217641, 2022; read in full.) Leaving all of that out is what most sets a game like this apart.
  • Endings go best when the screen itself ends. In interviews with 27 families and a diary study of 28 more (children 1–5), most transitions away from screens went fine (59% neutral, 19% positive, 22% upset). They went better with routines, natural stopping points, and when the technology ended the session rather than the parent. A parent's two-minute warning made children more upset. Autoplay and suggested videos caused many of the fights. (Hiniker et al., CHI 2016, "Screen Time Tantrums"; UW News and the lab's page.) This matches what we saw with Eliot: he accepts Reksio going to sleep.
  • Fantastical, fast content can briefly dull self-control. After 9–20 minutes of fast, fantastical cartoons (physically impossible events), 4-year-olds did worse on executive function tasks than after slow, realistic shows, drawing or play. In the 2015 follow-up, fantasy mattered more than pace. These are short-term effects in small laboratory studies. An unpublished thesis that tried the same with tablet games did not find the effect. (Lillard & Peterson, Pediatrics 128(4):644–649, 2011; Lillard et al., Developmental Psychology 51(6):792–805, 2015; abstracts only.)
  • Screens and sleep. In preschoolers, heavy screen use goes with shorter and poorer sleep, and poorer sleep with more behaviour problems (correlational; a review of 13 studies, Merín et al., European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 2024; abstract only).
  • What makes an app worth a child's time: the child is actively thinking (not just tapping), engaged rather than distracted, the play is meaningful, and it is shared with others. (Hirsh-Pasek et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 16(1):3–34, 2015; summaries only.)

What follows for us (our reading)

  • A short day suits a toddler. 5 minutes is well within the guidance. A day of about 5–8 minutes needs no limit beyond the game's own ending.
  • The ending is designed to be a natural stopping point. Reksio's bedtime, the same every play, with no autoplay and no "next", is what the transitions research says works. It must not become a warning: a cuckoo each hour is part of the world, not a countdown. Whether a visible evening calms Eliot or sounds like "two more minutes" isn't known; watch him play.
  • Play together. Both the AAP and the research favour a parent beside the child. The game should give the parent things to point at and laugh at, and README should say so, not present the game as something to hand a child to play alone.
  • Not a bedtime story. Reksio's bedtime could invite using the game to settle a child before bed, which the AAP advises against (no screens in the hour before bed). Play is for the daytime; the evening in the game is Reksio's, not the child's. README says so.
  • Not a way to calm a child. Don't present the game as one.
  • Gentle slapstick, little magic. Reksio's gags are physical comedy with a dog in a real yard, which keeps us on the slow, realistic side of the Lillard studies. Keep impossible events rare. (Those studies are about TV, and they measured only the time just after watching.)
  • No manipulation at all, including the subtle kinds: characters asking the child to stay, things to collect, rewards for coming back, time pressure.
  • Not an educational app, and we make no claim that it teaches. Its worth is shared laughter and a calm ending, which none of these studies measure. Only watching families play will tell.
